Hi Sara & Kyle,

Thanks again for the convo today - great to meet you both. Quick recap + proposed next steps so we have alignment: 

- Key goals you articulated: reduce cart abandonment with a fast, personalized recommendations experience; keep per-recommendation latency < 120ms P50; and cap monthly inference spend to a predictable budget during MVP.
- Current MVP traffic estimate (from the deck you shared): ~2M prediction requests/day during peak campaign, average prompt size ~600 tokens (system + user + metadata), expected output ~80 tokens.
- Important constraints: PII filtered at edge, cannot send raw user IDs to shared third-party endpoints; will need Private deployment or dedicated tenancy depending on procurement.

Action items:
1) I'll confirm our rough unit economics and give a target $/1M tokens range for you to evaluate vs budget.
2) Can you confirm the expected concurrency distribution? You mentioned bursts up to ~400 rps for 10-15 minutes, with a steady background of ~35-50 rps. Also please attach the traffic spreadsheet you referenced.
3) Looping in Marissa for pricing and Ben for procurement if/when we need redlines.

I attached a pricing summary and a quick worksheet where I'll place our cost assumptions. If you confirm the concurrency shape and daily token distributions we can give a more precise committed capacity vs pay-as-you-go comparison.

Best,

Thanks Camila - appreciate the summary. A couple clarifications and the traffic file attached.

- Confirming numbers from the deck: expected peak ~2M requests/day (campaign windows), average prompt in/out tokens ~680 tokens total (we run longer system prompts with product context).
- Concurrency shape: baseline ~40 rps (24/7), predictable marketing bursts up to 420 rps for ~12-20 minute windows (roughly 3-4 times per day during campaign peaks). Bursts are fairly spiky but with a short tail.
- Budget: for MVP pricing we're targeting a target spend level that maps to roughly $2,000-$3,500 per month for inference. If possible, give unit economics expressed as $ per 1M tokens so we can model three scenarios (low/expected/high).
- Question: how much savings should we expect from continuous batching vs naive per-request calls given our token sizes and burst shape? Is there a rule-of-thumb for concurrency thresholds where batching starts to meaningfully reduce per-token cost?

Attached: acme_mvp_traffic_estimates.xlsx

Thanks,
Sara Mason
Head of Growth | Acme Retail
sara.mason@acmeretail.com

From: Camila Reyes <camila@redwood-inference.com>
To: Sara Mason <sara.mason@acmeretail.com>, Kyle Turner <kyle.turner@acmeretail.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood-inference.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood-inference.com>
Date: Tue, 21 Jul 2026 09:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery - Redwood + Acme (post-call recap & next steps)

Sara - great, thanks for the file and the clarity. Below are the initial unit economics and batching assumptions based on the numbers you shared. These are conservative estimates; Aditya (cc'd) can validate technical assumptions.

Unit economics (ballpark) - for MVP traffic (~2M req/day, ~680 tokens per request, output 80 tokens):
- Total tokens per request (avg): 760 tokens.
- Daily token volume: ~1.52B tokens/day (2M * 760).
- Monthly tokens (30d): ~45.6B tokens.

Pricing scenarios ($ per 1M tokens):
- PAYG public-hosted baseline (example): $8-$12 per 1M tokens - this is public multitenant pricing equivalent for similar open models.
- Dedicated / committed capacity: $4-$7 per 1M tokens depending on commit level and quantization (int8) profile.
- Private/on-prem with long-term contract: $3.5-$6 per 1M tokens depending on host infra and support SLAs.

Mapping to your target budget ($2k-$3.5k/month):
- At $5 / 1M tokens you'd get ~400M tokens/month for $2k, ~700M tokens/month for $3.5k - far below the ~45.6B we estimate for the campaign. In short: the current campaign load is well outside that budget unless we materially reduce token counts or scope.

Continuous batching and concurrency assumptions - what to expect: 
- For long prompts (600-800 tokens) and short-ish outputs (~80 tokens), continuous batching yields modest per-token savings at low concurrency but becomes significant as request-level concurrency increases.
- Rule-of-thumb: with average prompt sizes like yours, batching starts to materially reduce per-token inference cost when sustained concurrency > ~60-80 concurrent requests (higher for smaller prompts). The crossover point (where dedicated capacity + batching < PAYG) typically sits around sustained hundreds of rps depending on your model choice and quantization.
- For your burst pattern (baseline 40 rps, spikes to 420 rps for ~15 mins): during spikes we can achieve good batching efficiency and reduce peak unit cost by ~20-40% compared to naive single-request serving (assuming continuous batching + pooling across requests). However, because spikes are short, the overall monthly cost delta depends heavily on duty cycle - i.e., how often those spikes occur.

Near-term recommendations:
1) Re-evaluate prompt templates: can we reduce system prompt size or move static context to K/V cache? Reducing 100-200 tokens per request massively reduces spend.
2) Consider a hybrid approach for MVP: hosted PAYG for baseline low-traffic periods + short-term Dedicated pool sized for campaign peaks (can autoscale with burst windows). This gives predictability for peak cost while avoiding large committed spend for steady-state.
3) If you want a committed quote, share a 7-14 day sample of real traffic (timestamps + token counts) so we can run a cost projection and recommend a commit size.

Attaching the quick worksheet with the above numbers filled in. I'll let Aditya comment on the continuous batching assumptions and expected % savings for your exact shape.

Best,
Camila

Attachments: redwood_pricing_summary.pdf, acme_mvp_traffic_estimates.xlsx

Sara - quick technical note on continuous batching and tradeoffs for your workload: 

1) Continuous batching behavior:
- Our runtime maintains short windows (tunable, e.g., 5-50ms) to accumulate in-flight requests for a given model/sequence-length bucket. For large prompts (~700-800 tokens), the service is compute-bound, so batching many inputs into a single kernel call yields good amortization of attention costs.

2) Expected savings & latency tradeoffs:
- For 40 rps steady-state: batching window will often be empty or have 1-2 requests; savings are minimal (single-digit %).
- For sustained 200-400 rps spikes: we typically see batching windows fill to dozens of requests within 10-30ms for the same model/config, giving ~25-45% reduction in per-token GPU time (which roughly maps to similar cost savings on Dedicated pools).
- Tail latency: to maintain P50 <120ms we recommend an aggressive batching timeout (<= 20ms) and prioritizing smaller latency-sensitive requests onto a lower-latency pool if needed. We can route high-priority calls to a low-latency instance class (with lower batching efficiency) and batch lower-priority ones.

3) Concurrency buckets and model variants:
- If you choose an int8 quantized model on dedicated pool, memory footprint drops and batch sizes can be larger per-GPU, improving batching efficiency further.
- We can provide modeled simulations if you share the token-per-request distribution by minute for a week. That will let us output expected per-minute batch sizes, mean latency, and estimated GPU-hours (and therefore cost).

Next steps (technical):
- If you're open, we'll run a 7-day simulator using your attached sheet and return a short report with expected batching efficiency and cost curves (no infra changes required).
- If acceptable, discuss a short pilot with a limited dedicated pool for two weeks covering campaign windows so you can validate latency and costs.

Happy to chat through the simulator assumptions - I'm free Wed/Thu afternoon PT.

Thanks,
Aditya Rao
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
